sandhi.note: a + ā → ā. Then आज्ञप्तः before the voiced v becomes आज्ञप्तो (हशि च, 6.1.114); likewise वध्यो before b.
-aḥ before a: the visarga becomes u, a + u gives o, and the following a is absorbed (avagraha).

samasa.sense: on the open sea (महत् takes the form महा- as first member of a karmadhāraya)

morph.note: From the causative of √ज्ञा, which has a short vowel (ज्ञपयति ‘to make known, command’). Pāṇini allows the irregular participle ज्ञप्त beside the regular ज्ञपित. With वध्यः: ‘ordered (to be) one to be killed’.
A gerundive (kṛtya) in -य: ‘to be killed, deserving death’. Grammarians attach it to √हन्, whose substitute stem वध- appears in several forms.
√स्था + क्त: the root vowel ā becomes i before the participle ending (स्थित).

mantras.anvaya: क्रुद्धेन राज्ञा च वध्यः (इति) आज्ञप्तः, बन्धगतः अपि वा, महार्णवे पोते स्थितः वातेन आघूर्णितः वा … (नरः — 12.29)
mantras.anvaya_en: More phrases in apposition to नरः (12.29): a king’s sentence, prison, and a storm at sea.
mantras.lit: or ordered by an angry king (as one) to be killed, or even gone into bonds; or tossed about by the wind while standing in a ship on the great ocean,
mantras.tr: condemned to death by an angry king, or lying in chains; or tossed by the gale on a ship on the great ocean,

comm.t: Three more perils: a death sentence from an angry king, imprisonment, and a ship caught in a storm. The order runs from danger at the hands of authority to danger from nature.
The frame gives this list a living example: Suratha, who hears these words, has lost his kingdom to enemies and his own ministers (1.5–9). The perils are not abstract for him.

sandhi.note: Inside the compound ā + a → ā and i → y before a (अभि + अर्दित → अभ्यर्दित). At the word boundary -aḥ + a → -o’.

samasa.sense: in every kind of distress (the feminine सर्वा takes its masculine form सर्व- as first member)
in agony, racked by illness or wounds

morph.note: Locative plural of the present participle पतत् (√पत् + śatṛ): with शस्त्रेषु a locative absolute, ‘weapons falling’, i.e. ‘while weapons fall’.
अभ्यर्दित is the past participle of अभि + √अर्द् ‘to oppress, torment’, with iṭ.

mantras.anvaya: भृशदारुणे संग्रामे शस्त्रेषु पतत्सु च अपि, घोरासु सर्वाबाधासु (वा), वेदनाभ्यर्दितः अपि वा … (नरः — 12.29)
mantras.anvaya_en: A locative absolute (शस्त्रेषु पतत्सु) with its setting (संग्रामे), a locative of circumstance (सर्वाबाधासु), and a last participle in apposition to नरः.
mantras.lit: and even when weapons are falling in an exceedingly terrible battle, in all terrible afflictions, or even tormented by pain,
mantras.tr: when weapons rain down in a fearful battle, in every dire calamity, or racked with pain —

comm.t: The list closes with battle, with every kind of calamity, and with bodily pain. सर्वाबाधासु widens it to anything not yet named, echoing the gods’ request for ‘the calming of all afflictions’ (सर्वाबाधाप्रशमनं, 11.39) and the Devī’s promise in 12.13.
A modern reading: the last item is the most private — pain, where no enemy is involved at all. The promise reaches from the battlefield to the sickbed.

sandhi.note: a + e → ai; the final t of एतत् becomes c before c.
-aḥ before the voiced m becomes -o; likewise दस्यवो before v.
-āḥ before a voiced consonant: the visarga becomes y, and the y is dropped before a consonant, leaving -ā.

samasa.literal: those whose first is the lion
samasa.sense: lions and the other wild beasts named in 12.26

morph.note: Passive optative of √मुच्: stem मुच्य- with the ātmanepada optative ending -ईत (a + ī → e). The optative states what follows as a rule: ‘(such a) man would be freed’.
Nominative singular masculine of the present participle स्मरत् (√स्मृ, guṇa stem स्मर-). The participle carries the condition: ‘(if) remembering’.
Nominative plural of the u-stem दस्यु: guṇa of the stem vowel (u → av) before -अः.

mantras.anvaya: मम एतत् चरितं स्मरन् नरः संकटात् मुच्येत। मम प्रभावात् सिंहाद्याः दस्यवः तथा वैरिणः (12.30: स्मरतः … दूरात् एव पलायन्ते)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line gives the main clause for the whole list of 12.25b–28: the man in any of those perils, remembering the story, is freed. The second opens a new sentence whose verb is पलायन्ते in 12.30.
mantras.lit: Remembering this story of mine, a man would be freed from danger. Through my power, lions and the rest, robbers, and likewise enemies
mantras.tr: whoever remembers this story of mine is set free from peril. By my power, lions and other wild beasts, robbers and enemies
mantras.tr_note: The optative मुच्येत is rendered as a plain present (‘is set free’): it states what happens, not a wish.

comm.t: The long sentence begun in 12.25 reaches its verb: the person in any of the dangers listed, remembering (स्मरन्) the Devī’s story, is freed. स्मरन् governs the whole list: in every peril named, what saves is remembering.
The Śākta tradition sets this verse beside the Devī’s promise in 11.54–55 (‘whenever trouble arises … I shall descend’): the remembered story is how she comes to the one in trouble.
A modern reading: the verse says ‘remembering’, not ‘reciting’. In a burning forest or a storm at sea no book or ritual is to hand; what one carries inside is what is left.

sandhi.note: Final t becomes d before a vowel.
Visarga before c becomes s, and s becomes ś next to c.
Final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra.

morph.note: परा + अय- with the r of the prefix changed to l (a rule of Pāṇini for the prefixes परा and परि before √अय्): पलायते ‘runs away’. Ātmanepada present, third person plural.

स्मरत् (√स्मृ + śatṛ) in the ablative singular: verbs of fleeing and fearing take the ablative of what is fled. It could also be read as a genitive (‘of one remembering’), but the ablative with पलायन्ते is the natural construction.

mantras.anvaya: (सिंहाद्याः दस्यवः तथा वैरिणः — 12.29) मम चरितं स्मरतः दूरात् एव पलायन्ते।
mantras.anvaya_en: The verb and its ablative complete the sentence begun in 12.29b.
mantras.lit: flee even from afar from one remembering my story.
mantras.tr: flee far from anyone who remembers my story.

comm.t: The half-verse that ends the Devī’s speech, begun at 12.2. Beasts, robbers and enemies do not merely fail to harm the one who remembers her story: they flee from far off (दूरात् एव), before any encounter.
The Gita Press pāṭha counts this half-śloka as a mantra of its own (an ardha), as the chapter colophon’s count requires. With it the Devī’s phalaśruti, spoken in her own voice, is complete.

sandhi.note: Visarga after i, before a vowel, is sounded as r.

mantras.anvaya_en: Subject and verb: a speaker label.

comm.t: Medhas takes up the narration again after the Devī’s speech (12.2–30), still speaking to King Suratha and the merchant Samādhi. He tells how the Goddess vanished and the gods returned to their places, and then draws the lesson of the whole story for the king.
